title: Configuration Paths of AI-Driven Urban Green Innovation: A Dynamic Qualitative Comparative Analysis Based on the TOE Framework
summary: Artificial intelligence (AI) has increasingly been recognized as an important driver of green innovation, yet how cities leverage AI capabilities to achieve green innovation outcomes under different configurations of conditions remains insufficiently understood. This study develops a configurational framework based on the technology–organization–environment (TOE) perspective and applies dynamic qualitative comparative analysis (QCA) to panel data from 35 Chinese cities, comprising municipalities directly under the central government, provincial capitals, and sub-provincial cities, during 2019–2023. The results identify three configurations associated with high urban green innovation. AI Technology Development and AI Institutional Support consistently emerge as core conditions across all configurations, while AI Organizational Scale is identified as a recurring peripheral condition. The findings further reveal causal asymmetry between high and non-high levels of urban green innovation, showing that individual AI-related conditions alone are insufficient to achieve high green innovation outcomes without complementary conditions. Dynamic analysis indicates that the overall configurational structures remain relatively stable over time, although the consistency of individual configurations varies as AI applications and policy environments evolve. This study advances research on AI and green innovation by demonstrating that AI-driven urban green innovation depends on the interplay among multiple conditions and involves both stable foundational factors and evolving complementary conditions.

title: Does accounting reflect or construct the business reality?: Empirical evidence from Hungarian accounting professionals
summary: This study examines how Hungarian accounting professionals interpret the role of financial statements in practice, whether they primarily view them as objective information tools that faithfully reflect economic events, or as professional practices that actively shape business reality through regulation and professional judgment. The empirical analysis is based on questionnaire data collected in July 2025 from members of two Hungarian accounting professional organizations, yielding 491 valid responses. Using non-parametric statistical methods, the study tests three hypotheses. The “equally correct but different” representation of economic events under IFRS and Hungarian accounting regulation (H1) and the perceived potential for deliberate distortion through valuation practices (H2) are examined using one-sample Wilcoxon signed-rank tests, while the social constructionist interpretation of accounting (H3) is explored through correlation analysis and principal component analysis (PCA). The results confirm H1 and H2, the majority of respondents accept the context-dependent relativity of accounting representations and clearly recognize the possibility of consciously shaping financial statements through valuation decisions. The items capturing the constructionist dimension show significant positive correlations, and PCA reveals a single, coherent factor. Overall, the findings indicate that Hungarian accounting professionals simultaneously embrace the normative “true and fair view” paradigm and a reflexive, social constructionist understanding of accounting.

title: Designing climate-adaptable agricultural supply chain networks with heterogeneous regions for perishable food systems in Turkey: A sustainable multi-echelon optimization approach
summary: This study develops a drought-aware agricultural supply chain network (AGSCN) for perishable crops at risk of drought, explicitly incorporating spatial zoning across heterogeneous farming regions with distinct production characteristics, including low- and high-risk zones. A bi-objective mixed-integer linear programming (BOMILP) model is formulated to simultaneously minimize total system cost and carbon emissions, thereby capturing economic efficiency and environmental sustainability considerations in perishable agricultural supply chain (AGSC) operations. The key contributions of this study are: (i) explicit integration of spatially heterogeneous production zones, enabling region-dependent production and allocation decisions under drought conditions; (ii) incorporation of region-specific drought disruption rates and yield factors to represent heterogeneous climate impacts on agricultural production capacity and supply chain performance; (iii) development of a unified BOMILP framework that jointly optimizes economic and environmental objectives in perishable AGSCNs; and (iv) a sequential multi-echelon distribution structure linking (iv) a sequential multi-echelon distribution structure linking farmers, local markets, wholesale markets, processing/export facilities, and consumers while accounting for capacity limitations and the operational characteristics of perishable agricultural products. A real-world case study of the Turkish tomato supply chain demonstrates the applicability of the proposed framework. The results show that increasing drought severity substantially changes regional sourcing patterns: the contribution of the high-risk Zone B to total supply decreases from approximately 45% under mild drought conditions to 22% under severe drought. In contrast, the model increases reliance on the more reliable Zone A, whose contribution reaches approximately 78% of the total network supply. These results demonstrate the model's ability to dynamically reallocate production and distribution flows in response to heterogeneous drought impacts while maintaining supply continuity. Overall, the findings highlight the importance of spatial diversification and adaptive sourcing strategies for improving the resilience and sustainability of perishable AGSCs under climate-induced disruptions.

title: Firm-Level Exposure to Climate Policy Uncertainty and Green Innovation: Nonlinear Evidence from Chinese Listed Firms
summary: Climate policy uncertainty may prompt firms to prepare for regulation while delaying irreversible green investment. We examine whether firm-level exposure is nonlinearly associated with green innovation. Exposure combines a news-based provincial climate policy uncertainty index with transition exposure extracted from annual-report management discussion and analysis sections. Using 13,972 firm-year observations from Chinese A-share listed firms over 2008–2024, we estimate models with firm and year fixed effects. Green invention patent applications exhibit an inverted U-shaped association with exposure. The estimated turning point is 0.686, and 13.52% of observations exceed it; a formal U-shape test supports the pattern. R&D results are consistent with a partial internal adjustment channel, but the conditional indirect association is indistinguishable from zero in the upper exposure tail. Tighter financing constraints weaken the positive marginal association and bring forward its reversal. The curve is more pronounced among large firms, while evidence for initial asset tangibility depends on its measurement. Several robustness checks preserve the nonlinear pattern, but stricter fixed effects and province-level clustering weaken the evidence. These observational findings suggest that innovation responses depend on both policy exposure and firms’ capacity to adjust.

title: The Role of Strategic Adaptation as a Mediator in the Relationship Between Digital Transformation, Innovation Capability, and MSME Competitiveness
summary: This study aims to analyze the influence of digital transformation and innovation capabilities on the competitiveness of MSMEs and examine the role of strategic adaptation as a mediating variable. This study uses a quantitative approach with a survey method of 230 MSME selected purposive sampling techniques. Data was analyzed using SEM-PLS. The results show that digital transformation and Innovation capabilities have a positive and significant effect on the strategic adaptation and competitiveness of MSMEs. In addition, strategic adaptation has a positive and significant effect on the competitiveness of MSMEs. Indirect effect test showed that strategic adaptation significantly mediated the relationship between digital transformation and the competitiveness of MSMEs and mediated the relationship between innovation capabilities and the competitiveness of MSMEs. The findings of the study confirm that increasing the competitiveness of MSMEs is not enough only through the adoption of digital technology and innovation development, but also requires the ability to adapt strategies, business models, marketing, operations, and human resource competencies to changes in the business environment. This study provides an implication that strengthening digital capabilities and innovation needs to be integrated with strategic adaptability so that MSMEs are able to build and maintain competitive advantages in a sustainable manner.

title: The impact of formal power and informal power on firm innovation: the asymmetric moderating roles of digital transformation
summary: Purpose The purpose of this paper is to examine the influence of formal power and informal power on firm innovation, with a particular focus on the moderating role of digital transformation. Design/methodology/approach The research sample consisted of Chinese A-share manufacturing firms between 2007 and 2024. Findings The research results indicate that both formal power and informal power have a significantly positive impact on firm innovation. However, the moderating effect of digital transformation on the impact of formal power and informal power is asymmetrical. In particular, digital transformation exerts a negative moderating effect on the relationship between formal power and firm innovation, whereas it exerts a positive moderating effect on the relationship between informal power and firm innovation. These results are subsequently validated through a series of robustness tests. Originality/value Firstly, this paper unpacks CEO power to examine the impact of formal power and informal power on firm innovation, rather than regarding it as an aggregate construct. Secondly, this paper contributes to the literature on digital transformation by empirically examining how digital transformation changes the impact of formal power and informal power on firm innovation. Thirdly, this paper contributes to the clarification of the relationship between CEO power and firm innovation by opening the “black box” of how digital transformation moderates the impact of formal power and informal power on firm innovation.

title: Step-Wise Holding Costs and Capacity Constraints in the EOQ Model: Accounting Valuation versus Operational Relevance
summary: The accuracy of the Economic Order Quantity (EOQ) model relies on the validity of its input parameters, particularly the holding cost. Conventional practices often adopt a full-costing accounting approach by incorporating fixed warehousing costs (rent, depreciation, salaries) into the decision variable. This practice is reinforced by financial reporting standards IFRS (IAS 2 Inventories) and the corresponding Indonesian standard PSAK 202 (effective 2024), which require the allocation of fixed production and warehousing overheads to inventory based on normal capacity. The objective of this study is to reconstruct the EOQ holding-cost parameter by separating those fixed warehousing overheads from the relevant variable costs that should drive replenishment decisions under warehouse capacity constraints. Utilizing conceptual modelling and numerical simulation, this research proposes a reconstruction of the EOQ model using a Step-Wise Cost Function that accounts for warehouse capacity constraints. Mathematical derivation and numerical simulation demonstrate that while the financial impact of parameter errors is dampened by the model’s robustness (cost increases of 6–25%), the operational distortion is significant. The inflation of holding costs leads to a surge in ordering frequency by up to 100%, triggering logistical inefficiencies and facility congestion. This study recommends a strict decoupling of financial reporting data from operational decision-making data to mitigate these hidden operational risks.

title: Charging and swapping technology innovation strategies in competitive EV supply chains: The impact of incentive policies and time-sensitive consumers
summary: The rapid expansion of the electric vehicle market, coupled with the limitations of traditional charging mode (CM), has driven the rise of swapping mode (SM), leading to coexistence and competition between the two. This study develops a competition model between CM and SM under dynamic power structures to explore optimal technology innovation strategies. By segmenting consumers based on time sensitivity, we examine how behavioral heterogeneity affects technology advancement, vehicle demand, and service adoption. Furthermore, we examine the impacts of different subsidy schemes on innovation and social welfare. Results show: (1) Technology levels in both modes peak under Nash game and are lowest under Manufacturer-led structures. While increased operator investment enhances innovation, an equitable cost-sharing mechanism is essential. (2) Consumer time sensitivity significantly shapes market outcomes, with highly time-sensitive consumers (H-consumers) generating an inverted U-shaped effect on social welfare. (3) Subsidies stimulate innovation in the emerging swapping mode but have limited marginal effects on the mature charging mode. There exists a critical threshold in the effectiveness of subsidies on social welfare. Specifically, consumer subsidies expand the early SM user base, while operator subsidies maximize social welfare. Notably, operator subsidies are more impactful when H-consumers dominate the market.

title: The Impact of Agency Costs on Investment Efficiency: Evidence from Overinvestment and Underinvestment in Borsa İstanbul
summary: Introduction: Agency costs can reduce resource allocation efficiency by distorting firms' investment decisions through conflicts of interest among managers, shareholders, and lenders. Therefore, examining the impact of agency costs on investment efficiency is a significant research area in the corporate finance literature. This study aims to analyze the impact of agency costs on firms' investment efficiency. Method: To determine the direction of investment inefficiency, overinvestment and underinvestment behaviors are examined through separate models. The study uses quarterly data from 24 firms listed on the BIST Industrial Index for the period 2015-2023. Investment efficiency was measured using the absolute value of residuals obtained from the expected investment model, in accordance with the approach of Biddle et al. (2009). Overinvestment and underinvestment were calculated using the positive and negative components of the residuals. Results or Findings: The study findings reveal that agency costs significantly affect investment efficiency, and this effect differs depending on the direction of investment divergence. Discussion or Conclusion: The results reval that agency costs not only increase overall investment inefficiency but can also influence both overinvestment and underinvestment behaviors of firms. These findings demonstrate that effective corporate governance mechanisms are crucial for optimizing investment decisions.

title: The impact of bond market liberalisation on corporate environmental greenwashing: empirical evidence from China
summary: Using the 2017 launch of China’s “Bond Connect” as a quasi-natural experiment, this study applies a difference-in-differences (DID) model to a sample of A-share listed companies over the period 2009-2024 to examine the causal impact of bond market liberalisation on corporate environmental greenwashing. Baseline results show that liberalisation significantly reduces environmental greenwashing. The finding remains robust to PSM, entropy balancing, placebo tests, and other robustness checks. Moreover, liberalisation operates through two primary channels. First, it strengthens external monitoring by attracting foreign investors and increasing media coverage. Second, it mitigates financing constraints by improving capital availability. Heterogeneity analysis shows this governance effect is more pronounced in firms with weaker internal controls, higher AI adoption, and larger bond issuance volumes. This research extends the corporate finance literature on capital market internationalisation. It also provides empirical evidence that financial opening can support substantive corporate green transitions in emerging markets.

title: Reshaping corporate accountability in the digital economy: the ‘digital regulatory chill’ effect and investment protection barriers in ASEAN
summary: ASEAN governments are trying to regulate digital platforms, and investment treaties may be making that harder. Investment protection clauses in CPTPP, in the signed but unratified EVIPA, and in surviving bilateral investment treaties give multinational platforms a legal toolkit for resisting the data governance and competition enforcement measures that Vietnam, Indonesia, Singapore, and Thailand are building. Through doctrinal analysis across these four jurisdictions, the article identifies what it calls ‘digital regulatory chill’: a structural vulnerability to the constraint of host-state regulatory capacity, one that operates through treaty architecture rather than the threat of any particular arbitral claim. The argument is not that platforms routinely win disputes. It is the credible possibility of a claim, combined with limited institutional capacity and the irreversibility of digital market tipping, that is plausibly capable of influencing regulatory decisions. Four conflict vectors are examined: data localization, algorithmic transparency mandates, competition enforcement, and interoperability obligations. Existing safeguards are a patchwork designed for brick-and-mortar economies and ill-suited to platform governance. The article proposes a four-level reform strategy, from joint interpretive statements to investor obligation clauses in a DEFA protocol, to address the vulnerability this architecture creates for ASEAN states seeking to govern digital platforms.

title: Strategic Planning as a Cornerstone of Quality Assurance in Higher Education: A Coupling Model with ISO 21001, ESG/ASG-QA, and Evidence Dashboards
summary: This paper argues that strategic planning is the engine of quality assurance (QA) in higher education when it is explicitly coupled with recognized reference frameworks and operational evidence infrastructures. Drawing on an integrative synthesis of the Standards and Guidelines for Quality Assurance in the European Higher Education Area (ESG), the African Standards and Guidelines for Quality Assurance (ASG‑QA), and ISO 21001:2018, we propose a “coupling model” that links mission and goals to process inventories, risk registers, and role‑based dashboards. We illustrate the model with the Cameroonian policy context namely the Education and Training Sector Strategy 2023–2030 (ETSS 2030) and the National Development Strategy 2020–2030 (NDS30) and with regional QA reforms (e.g., South Africa’s QAF). We show how institutional KPIs can be derived from sector targets and embedded in Plan‑Do‑Check‑Act (PDCA) cycles supported by an EMIS 2.0 architecture focused on learning and accountability. Recent research on learning‑analytics dashboards and human‑centered provides design considerations for usability, equity, and pedagogical actionability. The contribution is a practical mapping procedure and dashboard specification that translate high‑level QA requirements into auditable processes, data elements, and governance artifacts feasible for universities in resource‑constrained settings.

title: Turning digital transformation into innovation: the roles of data-driven decision-making and innovation leadership in Vietnamese universities
summary: Purpose Drawing on the dynamic capabilities framework, contingency theory of decision-making and upper echelons theory, this study proposes and tests a dual moderated mediation model that explains how innovation leadership (IL) moderates the relationships between digital transformation (DT) and data-driven decision-making (DDDM) and between DDDM and innovation in universities. Specifically, the study clarifies how DDDM functions as a mechanism through which DT is translated into innovation performance. Design/methodology/approach This study employs partial least squares structural equation modeling to test the proposed model and its hypotheses using survey data from 108 universities in Vietnam. Findings The findings show that (1) DDDM fully mediates the relationship between DT and innovation, indicating that DT does not directly lead to innovation unless it is implemented through DDDM processes, and (2) IL positively moderates the sequential effect of DT, DDDM and innovation. Practical implications The findings suggest that universities should move beyond investing in digital technologies alone and should instead strengthen DDDM and IL. Doing so will enable universities to turn digital resources into product and process innovations, such as new courses and research projects, and to enhance staff capabilities, resource allocation and incentive systems. Originality/value This study contributes to the DT and innovation management literature by clarifying how DT leads to innovation through DDDM as a managerial and behavioral decision process and by identifying IL as a critical boundary condition shaping this transformation.

title: Artificial Intelligence (AI) in the Circular Economy: A Systematic Literature Review
summary: The transition from linear production and consumption to a circular economy (CE) requires organizations to manage complex information about products, materials, waste streams, and supply-chain activities. Artificial intelligence (AI) may support this transition, but research on its role across business and organizational contexts remains fragmented. This study systematically reviews how AI is applied to CE practices and identifies the main thematic areas in the literature. Following the Preferred Reporting Items for Systematic Reviews and Meta-Analyses (PRISMA) 2020 statement, Scopus was searched for English-language studies published up to 2025. After screening 301 records and assessing 56 full texts, 25 studies were included and analyzed through qualitative content analysis and thematic narrative synthesis. Four clusters emerged: AI-enabled circular operations and supply-chain transformation; resource recirculation, recovery, and loop closure; organizational and ecosystem capabilities for circular innovation and business-model transformation; and green marketing, stakeholder engagement, and corporate disclosure. Across these clusters, AI is reported primarily to improve visibility, prediction, classification, optimization, and coordination. Evidence is strongest for operational efficiency and waste-related applications, while support for higher-value circular strategies and system-level loop closure remains limited. AI should therefore be regarded as a conditional enabler rather than a sufficient driver of circular transformation; its contribution depends on circular objectives, organizational capabilities, human expertise, infrastructure, financing, governance, and interorganizational cooperation.

title: From Compliance to Risk-Based Auditing: Implementing the Audit Charter in Local Government
summary: This study analyzes the implementation of the Internal Audit Charter in strengthening the internal audit function and shifting supervisory practices from compliance-oriented to more risk-based and consultative audits in local governments. The study used a qualitative approach with a case study design at the Merauke Regency Regional Inspectorate. Nine informants were purposively selected, consisting of structural officials, internal auditors, PPUPD (Regional Audit Implementation Unit), and representatives of regional apparatuses as auditees. Data were collected through in-depth interviews, observation, and documentation and analyzed using the interactive model of Miles, Huberman, and Saldaña. The results show that the Audit Charter provides a clearer institutional framework regarding the mandate, authority, responsibility, and working relationships of internal audit. Its implementation is influenced by policy standards and objectives, resources, characteristics of the implementing organization, inter-organizational communication, implementer disposition, and the implementation environment. The findings also indicate a gradual shift towards more risk-based supervision and the development of assurance and consulting functions. However, limited human resources, the need for strengthening competencies and information technology, follow-up on supervisory results, and geographical conditions remain obstacles. This study confirms that policy implementation is a process that connects the formal mandate of the Audit Charter with changes in internal audit practices towards a more strategic function.

title: Analysis of Bank-Specific Variables Viewed by Investors: The Impact of Intellectual Capital, Good Corporate Governance, Liquidity, and Solvency on the Value of Banking Firms in Indonesia
summary: Bank-specific attributes may enhance profitability while conveying risks that reduce market valuation. Prior studies offer inconclusive findings and rarely examine net interest margin (NIM) as the mechanism linking intellectual capital (IC), good corporate governance (GCG), the loan-to-deposit ratio (LDR), and the capital adequacy ratio (CAR) to bank value. This study investigates their direct and NIM-mediated effects on price-to-book value (PBV). The sample comprises 26 Indonesian listed banks observed during 2018-2025, yielding 208 balanced panel observations. Both equations were estimated using random-effects Panel EGLS with White period robust covariance; indirect effects were evaluated using the robust Goodman test. IC and LDR positively affect NIM, whereas GCG and CAR do not. GCG and NIM positively affect PBV; IC and CAR are insignificant. LDR has a significant negative direct relationship with PBV, contrary to the hypothesized direction. NIM mediates only the LDR-PBV relationship: its positive indirect effect opposes the negative direct effect. The study's novelty is identifying this competitive mediation, showing that lending intensity improves valuation through interest-margin performance while investors simultaneously discount liquidity and credit risks.

title: Translating Green Intellectual Capital Into Green Business Strategy: Exploring the Roles of Sustainable Supply Chain Flexibility and Green Organizational Identity
summary: ABSTRACT This study investigates how green intellectual capital (GIC) drives the development of green business strategy (GBS) in the wine industry by examining the mediating roles of sustainable supply chain flexibility (SSCF) and green organizational identity (GOI). Drawing on the intellectual capital–based view (ICBV) and the natural resource–based view (NRBV), a mediation model is estimated using partial least squares structural equation modeling (PLS‐SEM) and complemented with importance–performance map analysis (IPMA). The empirical analysis is based on survey data collected from 201 Spanish wineries between September 2025 and February 2026. The findings reveal that GIC exerts a positive and significant direct impact on GBS, while also strongly influencing SSCF and GOI. In turn, both SSCF and GOI positively affect GBS and mediate the relationship between GIC and GBS, confirming their role as key organizational mechanisms through which environmental knowledge is translated into strategic action. The IPMA further shows that indicators associated with GIC and GOI exhibit the highest levels of importance in explaining GBS, whereas SSCF indicators, despite moderate performance, play a comparatively less influential role. This study makes three main contributions. First, it advances the literature by conceptualizing GBS as a primary strategic outcome of GIC. Second, it provides an integrated framework that explains how environmental knowledge is operationalized through supply chain flexibility and organizational identity. Third, it offers empirical evidence from the wine industry, emphasizing the importance of aligning intangible resources, organizational values, and operational capabilities to strengthen sustainability‐oriented strategies.

title: The Moderating Effect of Investor Trust on the Relationship between Disclosure of Environmental, Social, and Governance Practices and Sustainable Investment
summary: Sustainability issues globally have gained importance due to more objective and impartial sustainability reports, and investors' confidence in corporate reporting increases as they form opinions about their investments.The study aims to examine The Moderating Effect of Investor Trust on the Relationship between the Disclosure of Environmental, Social, and Governance (ESG) Practices and Sustainable Investment.A questionnaire survey of respondents from companies listed on the ASE in the Jordanian market was used to gather primary data.169 of the respondents in the sample were deemed suitable for statistical examination.The study employed partial least squares structural equation modeling for data analysis and hypothesis testing.The findings show that disclosure of Environmental, Social, and Governance (ESG) practices positively affects sustainable investment (SI).Nonetheless, while investor trust (IT) directly influences firm value, it significantly moderates the relationship between environmental, social, and governance (ESG) disclosure and corporate sustainable investment (SI).The results provide credence to the notion that IT positively impacts corporate SI through the disclosure of ESG practices in sustainability reports.These indices are particularly relevant to emerging markets, where they can serve as a reference for company initiatives aimed at sustainability, attracting investors, and improving performance.

title: High-value-added forest product exports, the digital economy, and the efficiency of forest ecological product value realization
summary: As ecological product value realization advances and green trade rules evolve, the relationship between high-value-added forest product exports and forest ecological product value realization efficiency has become increasingly important. Using a balanced panel dataset covering 31 Chinese provinces from 2015 to 2023, this study measures forest ecological-product value realization efficiency and employs a two-way fixed-effects model to examine the effects of high-value-added forest product exports and the digital economy. We further assess forestry industrial upgrading as a potential transmission channel and examine the moderating and threshold roles of the digital economy. The results show that both high-value-added forest product exports and digital economy development were both significantly and positively associated with the value-realization efficiency of forest ecological products, and the results remained consistent across multiple robustness checks. Channel testing showed that high-value-added forest product exports were significantly and positively associated with forestry industrial upgrading at the 5% level, supporting the industrial-structure channel. Interaction-term and threshold tests showed that higher levels of digital economy development strengthened the positive association between high-value-added forest product exports and the value-realization efficiency of forest ecological products; this association strengthened further when the digital economy index exceeded 0.2833 (approximately the 78.5th percentile of the sample). Heterogeneity analysis showed that the foregoing positive association was more pronounced in eastern regions, regions with stronger environmental regulation, and regions with greater forest-resource endowments; the positive association between digital economy development and the value-realization efficiency of forest ecological products was stronger in central and western regions and in regions with lower forest cover. The findings provide empirical evidence for promoting high-value-added forest product exports, harnessing the enabling role of digital trade, and efficiently realizing the value of forest ecological products.

title: Generasi Z dan Adopsi FinTech: Mengungkap Peran Niat Perilaku
summary: Financial Technology (FinTech) has significantly transformed the financial behavior of Indonesian society. However, its adoption rate remains uneven due to the influence of psychological and social factors such as attitude, convenience, social influence, and trust. This study aims to examine the role of behavioral intention to use as a mediating variable in the relationship between these factors and FinTech use behavior among Generation Z. The research employs a quantitative approach using primary data collected through convenience sampling of FinTech service users. Data were gathered through online questionnaires distributed via Google Forms and analyzed using Partial Least Squares Structural Equation Modeling (PLS-SEM) with SmartPLS software. The findings indicate that attitude and convenience have a positive and significant effect on behavioral intention to use, while social influence and trust do not show significant effects. Furthermore, attitude, convenience, and trust significantly influence use behavior. However, behavioral intention to use only mediates the relationship between attitude and use behavior and does not mediate the effects of the other variables. These findings contribute to a deeper understanding of the determinants of FinTech usage among Generation Z and provide practical implications for service providers and policymakers in promoting FinTech adoption and strengthening the digital economic ecosystem in Indonesia.

title: Faculty agility mediates the association between AI-enabled digital transformation and sustainable work outcomes in indian higher education
summary: Digital transformation powered by Artificial Intelligence (AI) technologies has triggered changes in teaching, research, and academic work practices of Higher Education Institutions (HEIs). While research has studied digitalization in higher education from various dimensions, scant literature has explored how adoption of AI technologies and organizational digital capabilities associated with faculty members’ sustainable work outcomes. This study aims to explore how perceived usefulness was positively associated with AI adoption and faculty agility, how digital readiness and organizational support positively associated with faculty agility, and how faculty agility positively related to sustainable work outcomes while partially mediating the relationship between dimensions of digital transformation and faculty’s sustainable work outcomes in Indian HEIs. Underpinned by the theoretical lens of Technology Acceptance Model, Socio-Technical Systems Theory, and Dynamic Capability Theory, this quantitative study used cross-sectional survey research design with primary data collected from 497 faculty members working in public and private HEIs in India. Structural equation modeling technique was used with IBM SPSS 29 and AMOS 28 software. Results indicated that perceived usefulness positively associated with AI adoption and faculty agility. Digital readiness and organizational support positively and significantly associated with faculty agility which in turn significantly associated with sustainable work outcomes while partially mediating the relationships between dimensions of digital transformation and sustainable work outcomes. Findings also indicated that organizational support was one of the strongest associated factors of faculty agility within digitally transforming academic ecosystems. This study contributes to AI-enabled digital transformation literature in higher education settings by addressing its practical significance for university administrators and policy-makers toward building agile faculty workforce, faculty-supportive ecosystem, and digitally ready environment to sustain faculty’s technology-enabled work outcomes.

title: From Retail Scheduling to Supply-Chain Living Wages: An Agent-Based Simulation to Quantify the Business Value of Improving Job Quality for All
summary: Improving job quality for frontline workers is widely recognized as both a moral imperative and a potential source of competitive advantage, yet most organizations continue to underinvest in working conditions. A central reason is the absence of tools capable of translating job quality improvement into measurable and context-specific financial outcomes that decision-makers can act on. This paper reviews evidence linking job quality to firm-level financial performance and identifies limitations of conventional analytical tools that prevent organizations from making informed investment decisions. We argue that agent-based simulations can address these limitations by modeling heterogeneous agents whose behaviors and interactions allow organizational dynamics to emerge from the bottom up. We illustrate this approach through the Job-Quality Impact Explorer (JQIE), a proof-of-concept simulation focused on frontline workers in a retail environment that traces the causal chain from four job quality inputs (pay level, guaranteed minimum hours, advance scheduling notice and shift-swap ability) through worker satisfaction and behavior to company financial outcomes. Simulated results under the model’s current assumptions show that a company providing none of these benefits may earn as much as 35% less annual profit relative to an otherwise identical company providing all four benefits. Sensitivity analysis confirms that this pattern holds robustly across a range of assumptions about the underlying satisfaction effect. We discuss JQIE’s potential as a decision-support framework, its limitations, and ongoing efforts to expand this work to improve the working conditions of millions of workers in global supply chains.

title: Unintended Welfare Implications of Mandatory ESG Disclosure and Ethical Certification
summary: This dissertation examines how disclosure, transparency, and ethical interventions shape market behavior within the broader context of environmental, social, and governance (ESG) practices. The first chapter studies sustainability transparency in a product-market competition model in which customers and investors differ in their responsiveness to firms’ ESG performance. It shows that transparency can reduce unit-level externalities while increasing aggregate externalities through expanded production and market segmentation, with important implications for social welfare and empirical research design. The second chapter extends this analysis from sustainability disclosure to ethical declarations, which can be understood as a governance-oriented form of ESG communication. Using a controlled market experiment, it examines whether public ethical statements affect seller reporting, buyer trust, and auction outcomes. The findings show that such declarations can influence buyers’ beliefs and the terms of trade even when they do not materially reduce seller misreporting. Together, the chapters demonstrate that both sustainability transparency and governance-oriented ethical disclosures can produce unintended consequences when market participants respond strategically and heterogeneously to information.

title: Influence of Short Selling Mechanism on Equity Pledge Behaviors of Major Shareholders: Evidence from China’s A Share Market
summary: The margin trading system launched in March 2010 is an important measure of financial innovation in China’s capital market, which brings short selling mechanism to the securities market. Short selling mechanism can improve the pricing efficiency of the stock market, accelerate the spread of negative news of listed companies, increase the downward pressure on their stock prices, and thus may reduce the equity pledge behaviors of major shareholders. By using quarterly data from 2010 to 2020 of A-share listed companies in Shanghai and Shenzhen stock exchanges, this paper empirically examines the inhibitory effect of short selling mechanism on equity pledge behaviors of major shareholders. The paper shows that short selling mechanism significantly inhibits the equity pledge behaviors of major shareholders and reduces the times and ratio of their equity pledge, and that the greater the power of short selling, the more obvious the inhibitory effect. In addition, short selling mechanism can restrain the tunneling practice of major shareholders, improve the equity balance degree of the companies, and therefore reduce the equity pledge behaviors of major shareholders. The findings of the paper enrich the empirical results of short selling mechanism in corporate governance, and also help deepen the understandings of the motives and influence factors of large shareholders’ equity pledge.

title: Marker-Less Augmented Reality as a Catalyst for Digital Transformation in Furniture SMEs Through an Extension of the Cognitive–Affective–Conative Theory
summary: While large firms of furniture industry have integrated technologies such as Augmented Reality (AR) to allow consumers to visualize 3D furniture in their own spaces before purchase, small and medium-sized enterprises (SMEs) have not yet fully optimized this technology. This study examines consumer acceptance of AR in the SME furniture sector by developing a prototype product catalog website that integrates AR functionality. It also introduces a new theoretical model, the Cognitive, Affective, Evaluative, Conative (CAEC) model, which extends the traditional Cognitive, Affective, Conative (CAC) theory by adding an evaluative stage. A mixed-methods approach is employed, combining semi-structured interviews and surveys with the AR-enabled website prototype. The research contributes theoretically by introducing the CAEC model and provides a refined framework for understanding technology adoption. Practically, it guides SMEs in enhancing consumer engagement and purchase intentions through the use of AR.

title: Digital Transformation in Small-scale Food Enterprises: How Young Women Leverage Social Commerce to Globalize Local Specialties
summary: This study examines how digital transformation contributes to market expansion performance among young women-led small-scale food enterprises in Vietnam, with social commerce proposed as a mediating mechanism and digital literacy as a moderating capability. Drawing on the Resource-Based View and Dynamic Capabilities Theory, the study conceptualizes market expansion performance as the progressive broadening of customer base and geographic market reach through digital channels, extending beyond conventional export-based measures of internationalization. Data were collected from 227 young women entrepreneurs operating small-scale food enterprises producing local agricultural and food specialties across Vietnam, and the proposed model was tested using Partial Least Squares Structural Equation Modeling (PLS-SEM). The results indicate that digital transformation has a significant positive effect on both social commerce and market expansion performance, and that social commerce partially mediates the relationship between digital transformation and market expansion performance. Digital literacy significantly and positively moderates both the digital transformation–social commerce relationship and the social commerce–market expansion performance relationship, indicating that entrepreneurs’ digital competencies strengthen the conversion of digital capabilities into market-facing outcomes. These findings extend the application of the Resource-Based View and Dynamic Capabilities Theory to digitally enabled market expansion in an emerging-market, gender-specific, and place-based entrepreneurial context. The study offers practical implications for young women entrepreneurs, provincial authorities, and national policymakers seeking to strengthen digital capabilities and social commerce practices to help geographically and culturally rooted local specialties reach broader domestic and international markets.

title: Does gender influence ESG reporting practices of agri-food companies? Evidence from Asian economies
summary: Abstract ESG risks pose serious risks to the brand and viability of agri-food companies, making them more vulnerable than other industries that necessitates ESG reporting practices. However, this study evaluated the ESG reporting practices of agri-food companies, which were not the focus of previous research. The study investigates how ESG motivations and obstacles influence ESG reporting practices of agri-food companies in Asian countries. The study also evaluates the influence of gender as a moderator in ESG reporting practices of agri-food companies. To reach the objectives we used the quantitative method which comprised a quantitative investigation of 400 experts (100 from each country). The study used PLS-SEM to evaluate the influence of ESG motivations and obstacles in ESG reporting practices while PLS-MGA was used for examining the gender influence grounded in agency theory, stakeholder theory and legitimacy theory. The study revealed that ESG motivations and obstacles have a positive and significant influence on ESG reporting practices in agri-food companies. Motivations and challenges together account for 69.84% of the variation in ESG reporting practices of agri-food companies. ESG motivations have a high degree positive influence on ESG reporting practices compared to ESG obstacles. The study also revealed that as a moderator, gender has no significant influence in ESG reporting practices of agri-food companies. Legal structures provide a helpful basis for the development of ESG disclosure practices, and the level of ESG reporting in Asian agri-food companies is increasing gradually. For regulators, policymakers, and companies operating in developing countries, this study has important implications. Our work also has intriguing real-world applications for regulators, policymakers, and other players in the Asian market. The study suggests that authorities and policymakers should take proactive measures to strengthen the implementation of the ESG reporting assessment in order to enhance ESG reporting practices.

title: The Auditor's Capacity to Employ Cybersecurity for Fraud Detection: The Influence of Training and Experience
summary: Indonesia, being a developing nation, possesses legislation regulating the compilation of financial accounts and requirements pertinent to auditors.The legislative system governing financial reporting is also evident in developed countries.Auditors in the Fourth Industrial Revolution possess cybersecurity expertise.This study seeks to clarify the influence of auditor experience and training on the auditor's ability to implement cybersecurity measures for identifying financial fraud, with professional skepticism acting as a moderating variable.The investigation encompassed 61 auditors from the Audit Board of Indonesia (BPK) Representative Office in North Sumatra Province.The results indicate a significant influence of auditor experience and training on the auditor's ability to utilize cybersecurity for identifying financial crime; however, professional skepticism does not operate as a moderating variable.This study's distinctiveness is rooted in the claim that auditors must have cybersecurity competencies to detect fraud in financial reporting.The auditor's proficiency in handling and reporting client money greatly affects their ability to detect fraud.Nonetheless, auditors must augment their competencies, especially considering the digital improvements in accounting, to provide highquality reports relevant to both current and future contexts.This will also serve as auditor branding in clients' perceptions and maintain the auditor's professional skepticism.

title: Cross-Substrate Phenomenal Comparison: A Typed Transformation-Transport Framework under Existential Uncertainty
summary: Comparing human, non-human animal, and artificial experience requires distinguishing whether a target has phenomenal experience from which aspects of its experience would be comparable if it does. Multidimensional profiles, behavioral similarities, and mechanistic correspondences provide important evidence, but do not by themselves settle measurement semantics, information loss, or the scope of cross-system inference. This paper proposes a typed transformation-transport framework whose basic comparison unit is a system-in-regime undergoing a specified intervention. Claims are distinguished by their targets: phenomenal existence, character, valence, perspectival organization, continuation, and token multiplicity. No universal human-centered phenomenal coordinate system is required, although each comparison requires an explicit local relational interface. The principal methodological object is a transport certificate separating observable causal correspondence, conditional phenomenal interpretation, and evidential updating about existence. Four propositions establish conditional non-identification under observational equivalence, a fiber criterion for query-preserving abstraction, guarded composition of set-valued constraints, and error propagation for metric interfaces. An exhaustively checked eight-state example shows that exact interventional correspondence can preserve one candidate phenomenal query while concealing a distinction relevant to another. A held-out intervention reveals the resulting model disagreement, but cannot empirically adjudicate it without an appropriate measurement connection. Bounded research protocols and a twelve-case conceptual regression suite operationalize the framework for human–animal–AI comparisons. The contribution is an integrated method for specifying and auditing transport claims, not a new sufficient condition for consciousness. In particular, the framework neither treats non-entailing evidence as worthless nor mistakes a formally valid conditional for an empirically established fact about experience. title: Determinants of Audit Report Lag: Evidence from Consumer Cyclicals Sector in Indonesia
summary: The purpose of this study is to investigate and present empirical data on the impact of company size, profitability, audit tenure, and Public Accounting company (PAF) reputation on audit report lag. The study utilizes secondary data, with the population consisting of consumer cyclical businesses that were listed between 2021 and 2025 on the Indonesia Stock Exchange (IDX). Based on the established criteria, 395 observations were obtained. SPSS version 31 was used to perform multiple linear regression analysis. The findings show that audit report lag is negatively impacted by firm size, negatively impacted by profitability, positively impacted by PAF reputation, and negatively impacted by audit tenure.

title: The Role of Fraud Risk Assessment in Moderating the Influence of Ethical Sensitivity and Religiosity on Public Sector Financial Reports in, Indonesia
summary: Financial reporting fraud remains a major challenge for the public sector in Indonesia, weakening fiscal accountability and eroding public trust. Therefore, individual moral attributes and their interaction with organizational mechanisms are very important to ensure that public sector financial reports are free from fraud. This article analyses ethical sensitivity and religiosity on public sector financial reports by placing fraud risk assessment as a moderator. By using a quantitative design, this research highlights that ethical sensitivity and religiosity are very important in preparing public sector financial reports. Sample data was collected from 400 public sector financial officials in Central Java, Indonesia, who were selected through purposive sampling. Data analysis uses Partial Least Squares Structural Equation Modelling (PLS-SEM). The research results show that ethical sensitivity and religiosity have a significant effect on reducing the tendency to defraud. Fraud risk assessment, at the same time, plays a pivotal role in strengthening those negative relationships, essentially pushing fraudulent behaviour further down. Taken together, these findings give solid empirical backing to the dual attribution framework, which basically argues that you cannot pull off effective fraud prevention by relying on just one side of the equation. It takes both; internal ethical inclinations and external organizational safeguards working in tandem, a kind of synchronized push from the inside out.

title: Toward AI-Enabled and Sustainability-Oriented Digital Transformation of Application-Oriented Universities: A Conceptual Framework and an Illustrative Smart Laboratory Pilot
summary: With the rapid advancement of digital technologies and the growing emphasis on high-quality and sustainable higher education, application-oriented universities are undergoing profound digital transformation. This conceptual study develops a sustainability-oriented framework grounded in Socio-Technical Systems Theory and the Dynamic Capabilities perspective, with China’s Four Futures initiative serving as a contextual lens for identifying key transformation domains. The framework integrates four institutional dimensions: faculty development, pedagogical innovation, institutional governance, and digital resource integration. It distinguishes existing digital foundations from prospective AI-enabled extensions and illustrates selected elements through an exploratory smart laboratory governance pilot. The pilot demonstrates how shared data standards, university–college workflows, laboratory management, safety management, teaching operations, and mobile visualization can be aligned with the proposed framework. However, this study does not claim improvements in teaching quality, operational efficiency, or resource utilization. Instead, it identifies key implementation conditions related to data quality, privacy, security, model validation, human oversight, accessibility, life cycle costs, and environmental impact. The framework provides a basis for future longitudinal and multi-institutional evaluation of responsible AI-enabled digital transformation in application-oriented higher education.
